meta.title: Who really said "True heroism is remarkably sober, very undramatic. It is not the urge to surpass all others at whatever cost, but the urge to serve others at whatever cost"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, this one is real. Arthur Ashe said it at Ohio Wesleyan's 1991 commencement; the earliest citation is the Delaware Gazette, 8 February 1993.

meta.ogDescription: Genuine Ashe - spoken at Ohio Wesleyan's 1991 commencement, first documented 8 Feb 1993. The 'courage to surpass' version is a misquote.

answer.sourceLine: Ashe said it from the commencement platform at Ohio Wesleyan University in Delaware, Ohio, to the class of 1991. Quote Investigator ↗ traced the line and concluded Ashe deserves credit for it: the earliest citation it found is The Delaware Gazette of 8 February 1993, printing this exact wording and crediting that address, and Bartlett’s Familiar Black Quotations (2013) dates the speech 12 May 1991.

source.excerpt: True heroism is remarkably sober, very undramatic. It is not the urge to surpass all others at whatever cost, but the urge to serve others at whatever cost.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗’s earliest citation is The Delaware Gazette of 8 February 1993 — the local paper of Delaware, Ohio, where Ohio Wesleyan sits — which prints this exact wording and reports that Ashe “told the Ohio Wesleyan University class of 1991 in his commencement address.”

Reader’s Digest carried it in August 1994 (vol. 145, no. 868) under “Points To Ponder,” with the source given only as “From a speech” — a mass-circulation printing that names no occasion at all (Quote Investigator ↗).

Bartlett’s Familiar Black Quotations (2013) is the citation that supplies the exact day, giving “Commencement speech, Ohio Wesleyan University [May 12, 1991]” (as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗).

Ashe’s own archive independently ties him to the college. The Schomburg Center’s finding aid lists an honorary doctorate from “Ohio Wesleyan” among his degrees, and notes that he “spoke at a number of commencement ceremonies, often as the recipient of an honorary degree” (NYPL finding aid ↗).
source.excerptNote: The wording as printed in The Delaware Gazette on 8 February 1993 and again in Bartlett’s Familiar Black Quotations in 2013. No published transcript or recording of the full address has been located, so the passage travels on its own in every citation.

source.rightsNote: These words come from a commencement address delivered on 12 May 1991 and first documented in print in February 1993 — far too recent for the public domain, which in the United States currently reaches works published before 1931. A speech is protected once it is fixed in a recording or manuscript, and delivering it at a public ceremony does not release it; quote the line briefly and with attribution, as here.

author.name: Arthur Ashe
author.heading: Who was Arthur Ashe?
author.metaLine: 1943–1993 · American tennis champion, author and activist
author.bio: Born in Richmond, Virginia in 1943, Arthur Ashe was the first African-American man to win a Grand Slam singles title — the US Open in 1968, followed by the Australian Open in 1970 and Wimbledon in 1975. Off the court he was a Washington Post columnist, an anti-apartheid campaigner arrested outside the South African embassy in 1985, and the author of A Hard Road to Glory, a three-volume history of the Black athlete published in 1988. He learned he was HIV-positive in September 1988, kept it private until a press conference on 8 April 1992, finished his memoir Days of Grace less than a week before his death on 6 February 1993, and was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously that June.

misattribution.heading: How it drifts
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is sound — it is the wording and the sourcing that go wrong. Because the line entered mass circulation through a quote column that named no occasion, it has wandered in several documented directions:

items.why: PassItOn prints “It is not the courage to surpass others at whatever cost, but the courage to serve others at whatever the cost,” swapping Ashe’s twice-repeated “urge” for “courage,” dropping “all” and adding a stray “the” (PassItOn ↗). Every citation Quote Investigator lists reads “urge.”

A widely shared Goodreads entry, taken from Alter Wiener’s memoir From a Name to a Number, loses the whole opening cadence — “remarkably sober, very undramatic” collapses into three words (Goodreads ↗).

The CBS series used it as a closing quote in a tightened form — “It’s not the urge to surpass others at whatever cost” — dropping “all” and contracting “It is” (Quotes.net ↗). Television is where a lot of people first met the line, and this is the version they met.

items.who: “From a speech” — or nothing at all
items.why: Reader’s Digest printed it in August 1994 with the source line “From a speech” and no occasion named (Quote Investigator ↗), and the most-copied Goodreads entry names no work whatsoever (Goodreads ↗). A real quote can still be badly sourced.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is genuinely Ashe’s, and it has a campus, a class and a date behind it: Ohio Wesleyan University, Delaware, Ohio, the class of 1991 — and it reads “the urge to surpass all others… the urge to serve others” (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: When Ashe faced the Ohio Wesleyan class of 1991, nobody in front of him knew he was ill. He had tested HIV-positive in September 1988 after surgery and chose to keep it private; he would not tell the public until a press conference on 8 April 1992 ↗, nearly a year after this speech. To a room of graduates, from a man who had spent a career being ranked, he defined heroism as the opposite of ranking — sober, undramatic, and measured entirely by what you are willing to give up for someone else.

The line then reached print in the worst possible way for anyone who later wanted to check it. Ashe died on 6 February 1993; two days later The Delaware Gazette, the paper of the town Ohio Wesleyan sits in, ran the quote and credited the 1991 address — the earliest citation Quote Investigator found ↗. Eighteen months after that, Reader’s Digest reprinted it under “Points To Ponder” with the source given only as “From a speech.” Most quote sites still carry it with no occasion attached at all.
context.detailsSummary: The paper trail, step by step
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s citation ladder runs 1993 → 1994 → 2001 → 2003 → 2013, and turns up no competing claimant and no earlier attestation (Quote Investigator ↗).

The specific date comes late: Bartlett’s Familiar Black Quotations (2013) is the citation that supplies “Commencement speech, Ohio Wesleyan University [May 12, 1991]” (as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗).
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its main Quotes section, sourced to the 1991 Ohio Wesleyan address and footnoted to Quote Investigator. The page has no Disputed or Misattributed section at all.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes "Arthur Ashe deserves credit for this statement. He spoke it during a commencement address in 1991 at Ohio Wesleyan University." Its earliest citation is the 8 February 1993 Delaware Gazette printing this exact wording; August 1994 Reader's Digest vol. 145 no. 868 ran it in "Points To Ponder" credited "From a speech"; 2013 Bartlett's Familiar Black Quotations cites "Commencement speech, Ohio Wesleyan University [May 12, 1991]". No competing attribution or earlier source is identified, and no variant wordings are noted.

Wikiquote lists the quote as the first item in its main "Quotes" section, sourced to "1991 commencement address at Ohio Wesleyan University" with a link to the Quote Investigator entry. Ashe's dates are given as 10 July 1943 - 6 February 1993. The page has no Disputed or Misattributed section; its only other sourced section is Days of Grace: A Memoir (1994).

Arthur Ashe was born 10 July 1943 in Richmond, Virginia and died 6 February 1993; he won the US Open (1968), Australian Open (1970) and Wimbledon (1975); he was diagnosed HIV-positive in September 1988 and publicly announced it on 8 April 1992; he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously on 20 June 1993; he finished the manuscript of Days of Grace less than a week before his death.

The Schomburg Center's finding aid for the Arthur Ashe archive (1959-2003, 20.6 linear feet) includes a Speaking Engagements series dated 1976-1992, states that "Ashe spoke at a number of commencement ceremonies, often as the recipient of an honorary degree," and lists Ohio Wesleyan among the institutions that awarded him honorary doctorates.

PassItOn prints the variant wording "True heroism is remarkably sober, very undramatic. It is not the courage to surpass others at whatever cost, but the courage to serve others at whatever the cost." credited to Arthur Ashe.

This Goodreads entry carries the truncated variant "True heroism is not dramatic. It is not the urge to surpass all others at whatever cost, but the urge to serve others at whatever cost." credited to Arthur Ashe as cited in Alter Wiener's From a Name to a Number: A Holocaust Survivor's Autobiography.

Quotes.net records Dr. Spencer Reid on the CBS series Criminal Minds delivering the line as a closing quote in the form "It's not the urge to surpass others at whatever cost, but the urge to serve others at whatever cost," credited to Arthur Ashe.
The widely copied Goodreads entry gives the standard wording credited to Arthur Ashe with no book, speech or source work named.

The Arthur Ashe Legacy at UCLA, hosted under the auspices of the Arthur Ashe Learning Center, presents Ashe as a conscience leader, humanitarian, educator and athlete and as the first African-American male tennis player to win a Grand Slam tournament.
